title: Emotional Intelligence
author: Daniel Goleman
theme: How well we understand and manage emotions, our own and other people's, shapes success at work and in life as much as raw intellect does.
summary: Daniel Goleman, a psychologist and science journalist, wrote this book to challenge a narrow idea of what it means to be smart. Schools and employers had long treated IQ as the main predictor of achievement, yet many people with high test scores struggle in their careers and relationships, while others of modest intellect thrive. Goleman argues that the missing ingredient is emotional intelligence: a set of learnable abilities for handling feelings well.

He grounds the argument in brain science. The emotional centres of the brain, especially the amygdala, can react to a perceived threat before the thinking parts of the brain have fully assessed it. This is why people sometimes erupt in anger or panic and later regret it. Goleman calls such moments emotional hijackings and explains that the rational brain can learn to moderate them.

Building on the work of researchers Peter Salovey and John Mayer, he describes five broad domains. The first is self-awareness, recognising a feeling as it happens. The second is managing emotions, such as calming anxiety or shaking off a bad mood. The third is self-motivation, which includes delaying gratification and persisting toward goals. The fourth is empathy, reading what others feel. The fifth is handling relationships, the social skill to influence, cooperate and resolve conflict.

Goleman shows how these abilities matter in many settings. In marriages, harsh criticism and contempt erode trust. At work, managers who give feedback badly damage morale, while teams with emotional harmony perform better. Poor emotional control is also linked to health problems and risky behaviour.

His most hopeful message is that emotional skills are not fixed at birth. Temperament can be reshaped by experience, and families and schools can deliberately teach children to name feelings, control impulses and solve conflicts. Developing these capacities, he concludes, benefits individuals and society alike.
takeaway: Notice your emotions as they arise, manage them before they manage you, and treat empathy and social skill as abilities you can practise and improve.

questions.q: What central claim does Goleman make about IQ?
options: IQ is irrelevant to any kind of success
IQ alone explains only part of why people succeed; emotional abilities matter greatly too
IQ can be raised easily through training
IQ is the best single predictor of a happy marriage
questions.why: Goleman argues that intellect is only part of the picture and emotional skills account for much of the difference in outcomes.

questions.q: What does Goleman mean by an 'emotional hijacking'?
options: A deliberate strategy to manipulate others
A long period of low mood
A sudden reaction driven by the brain's emotional centres before reasoning catches up
A technique for staying calm under pressure
questions.why: The term describes moments when the amygdala triggers an intense response before the thinking brain can weigh in.

questions.q: Which brain structure does Goleman highlight as central to fast emotional reactions?
options: The amygdala
The cerebellum
The spinal cord
The visual cortex
questions.why: He explains that the amygdala can sound an alarm and drive a reaction ahead of rational assessment.

questions.q: Which researchers' model of emotional intelligence does Goleman build upon?
options: Freud and Jung
Kahneman and Tversky
Maslow and Herzberg
Salovey and Mayer
questions.why: Goleman draws on the framework developed by psychologists Peter Salovey and John Mayer.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the five domains Goleman describes?
options: Self-awareness
Empathy
Technical expertise
Handling relationships
questions.why: The five domains are self-awareness, managing emotions, self-motivation, empathy and handling relationships; technical skill is not among them.

questions.q: What does self-awareness mean in Goleman's framework?
options: Recognising a feeling as it happens
Knowing your IQ score
Being aware of how others see your appearance
Planning your career ten years ahead
questions.why: Self-awareness is the foundational ability to notice and identify one's own emotions in the moment.

questions.q: The ability to delay gratification belongs mainly to which domain?
options: Empathy
Social skill
Self-awareness
Self-motivation
questions.why: Goleman links delaying gratification and persistence to motivating oneself toward goals.

questions.q: According to the book, what is empathy?
options: Agreeing with everyone to avoid conflict
Sensing and understanding what other people feel
Hiding your own emotions at work
Giving praise frequently
questions.why: Empathy is the capacity to read and understand the emotions of others.

questions.q: How does Goleman view the workplace consequences of emotional intelligence?
options: It matters only for salespeople
It has no measurable effect on teams
Skills like constructive feedback and team harmony improve performance
It mainly helps people avoid promotions
questions.why: He argues that emotionally skilled managers and harmonious teams achieve better results than those lacking these abilities.

questions.q: What is Goleman's view on whether emotional intelligence can be developed?
options: It is fixed at birth by genetics
It can be learned and strengthened, including through schools and families
It only develops after age forty
It can be gained only through medication
questions.why: His hopeful message is that temperament is not destiny and emotional skills can be taught and practised.
